power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

#### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 8 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (6), R history (2). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 112 columns across 16 data files.
#### Issues Identified

35 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

info.title: Registered Replication Report and Extension of Maas & Hox (2005), Sufficient Sample Sizes for Multilevel Models

text.text: The use of multilevel models in behavioral and social sciences has risen dramatically in the past several decades.
Researchers using these models often consult highly-referenced simulation studies when designing their own studies, especially for sample-size planning.
However, current literature suggests two issues with this practice.
First, recent work has called into the question the replicability of prior simulation studies.
Second, foundational simulations were conducted under relatively simple conditions, but researchers now use more complex models.
To address these issues, we conducted a replication and extension of Maas & Hox (2005), a study that is widely cited for sample size planning.
text.formatted: To address these issues, we conducted a replication and extension of <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas & Hox (2005)</ref>, a study that is widely cited for sample size planning.

text.text: We replicated their core findings, suggesting prior results may still inform sample size planning contingent on study design.
The extension introduced design features common in modern research, including multiple random slopes, cross-level interactions, and imbalanced Level-1 samples.

These conditions revealed that variance-component estimates are highly sensitive to ICC magnitude, imbalance, and Level-1 sample size, with acceptable coverage typically requiring Level-2 sample sizes N ≥ 100 and Level-1 sample sizes n ≥ 30.

Our findings converge on three general principles: random-effects are more difficult to appropriately estimate than fixed-effects, model complexity amplifies sample size demands, and imbalance can undermine coverage even in seemingly adequate designs.
Registered Replication Report and Extension of Maas & Hox (2005), Sufficient Sample Sizes for Multilevel Models
text.formatted: Registered Replication Report and Extension of <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas & Hox (2005)</ref>, Sufficient Sample Sizes for Multilevel Models

text.text: Nested data-such as students nested within classrooms or clients nested within therapists-are ubiquitous in the social-behavioral sciences, especially psychology.

Given the unique structure of these data, particular statistical methods are needed to appropriately analyze them in order to ensure accurate parameter estimation and subsequent inference (Bauer, McNeish, Baldwin, & Curran, 2020).
text.formatted: Given the unique structure of these data, particular statistical methods are needed to appropriately analyze them in order to ensure accurate parameter estimation and subsequent inference <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Bauer, McNeish, Baldwin, & Curran, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: One such method, multilevel modeling (Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002; Raudenbush, 1993), has become increasingly popular since the late 1980s as both an analytic tool for substantive psychological science and a topic of study in methodological development research (Snijders & Bosker, 2012; LeRoux, Cappelli, & Fikis, 2021; Liu & Rhemtulla, 2022; Tong, Zhang, & Zhou, 2021; Kim & Steiner, 2021).
text.formatted: One such method, multilevel modeling <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Raudenbush & Bryk, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Raudenbush, 1993)</ref>, has become increasingly popular since the late 1980s as both an analytic tool for substantive psychological science and a topic of study in methodological development research <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Snijders & Bosker, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">LeRoux, Cappelli, & Fikis, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Liu & Rhemtulla, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b50">Tong, Zhang, & Zhou, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kim & Steiner, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Multilevel models, also referred to as hierarchical, random coefficient, or mixed effects models, are a class of models designed to appropriately handle nested data.

Data are considered nested when the individual observations belong to a higher-order unit or entity that can be drawn exchangeably from its own population and possesses its own observable characteristics 1 .
Nested structures must be taken into account.

Treating the data as though they are not nested and proceeding with a 'standard' ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analysis has a tendency to downwardly bias coefficient standard errors and inflate false positive rates beyond their nominal level (Barcikowski, 1981).
text.formatted: Treating the data as though they are not nested and proceeding with a 'standard' ordinary least squares (OLS) regression analysis has a tendency to downwardly bias coefficient standard errors and inflate false positive rates beyond their nominal level <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barcikowski, 1981)</ref>.

text.text: Ignoring the nesting structure of a dataset obstructs the goal of conducting reliable science.

Multilevel models solve this problem by letting at least one term vary randomly 1 Because observations can be made at several points in a nesting hierarchy, the term 'level' is often used to help delineate which stratum in the nesting hierarchy a set of observations belong to (e.g., decisions nested within individuals are at Level-1, whereas characteristics about the individuals themselves come at Level-2).

Here, we use 'units' to describe cases that can be observed at either Level-1 (e.g., decisions) or Level-2 (e.g., individual), and 'levels' to describe a given stratum in the nesting hierarchy. across higher-level units, illustrated in the empty model below.

Here Y ij , the i-th value of a lower-level observation nested under the j-th higher-level unit, is being modeled as a function of a fixed intercept (γ * 00 ) that is constant across all higher-level units, a stochastic, normally distributed random effect (u * 0j ) that is unique to each higher-level unit, and an error term (e * ij ) assumed to be normally distributed, independent and identically distributed among lower-level units, and uncorrelated with the random effect (u * 0j ).
Level-1 error variance (σfoot_0 * e ) is assumed to be constant across higher-level units.
text.formatted: Level-1 error variance (σ<ref type="foot" target="#foot_0">foot_0</ref> * e ) is assumed to be constant across higher-level units.

text.text: Quantities from the empty model are notated with an asterisk.
This distinction will become increasingly important as additional concepts are reviewed.

The need for a multilevel model when analyzing nested data is frequently informed by the degree of similarity among lower-level observations within a higher level unit compared to those between such units.
This quantity can be measured via the intraclass correlation coefficient (ICC):
Where (τ * 00 ) is the random intercept variance and (σ 2 * e ) is the error variance.

The ICC is the proportion of total variance attributable to between-cluster variability, such that a larger ICC means that there is more of the total variation in a given variable is explained by differences between, rather than within, cluster.
It is critical to stress that the quantities in Equation 2 represent a partitioning of the total variance between-and withinhigher-level units.
Thus, ρ * in particular reflects the partitioning of all unconditional variance in Y ij .
Larger ICC values reflect stronger clustering and subsequently underscore a greater need to accommodate the nesting structure.

2  While there are other approaches to handling nested data (Hamaker & Muthen, 2020; McNeish, Stapleton, & Silverman, 2017), multilevel modeling has become particularly popular because of its versatility.
text.formatted: 2  While there are other approaches to handling nested data <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hamaker & Muthen, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">McNeish, Stapleton, & Silverman, 2017)</ref>, multilevel modeling has become particularly popular because of its versatility.

text.text: Multilevel models afford analysts the opportunity to include both Level-1 and Level-2 predictors in the same model, toggle random effects on and off as desired, and can accommodate more complicated modeling (e.g., growth curve modeling, cross-nested models, measurement models, etc.).

While this versatility makes multilevel modeling a powerful tool, it also means that virtually every aspect of multilevel modeling is more complex than traditional regression methods and gives researchers more to consider when selecting their analysis model and designing their studies (McNeish et al., 2017).
text.formatted: While this versatility makes multilevel modeling a powerful tool, it also means that virtually every aspect of multilevel modeling is more complex than traditional regression methods and gives researchers more to consider when selecting their analysis model and designing their studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(McNeish et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: This is especially true for determining sample sizes.
In multilevel modeling, researchers must determine the appropriate sample sizes for Level-1 and Level-2.

While closed-form, analytic solutions exist to help analysts compute sample size requirements for given effects (Scherbaum & Ferreter, 2009; Westfall, Kenny, & Judd, 2014; Moerbeek, van Breukelen, & Berger, 2000; Moerbeek & Maas, 2005; Spybrook, Kelcey, & Dong, 2016; Raudenbush & Liu, 2000; Murayama, Judd, & Sakaki, 2022), they are limited insofar that they primarily apply to simplistic model specifications that are less complex than the models substantive researchers typically want to use, or they rely on using problematic test statistics (Luke, 2017).
text.formatted: While closed-form, analytic solutions exist to help analysts compute sample size requirements for given effects <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Scherbaum & Ferreter, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Westfall, Kenny, & Judd, 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Moerbeek, van Breukelen, & Berger, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Moerbeek & Maas, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Spybrook, Kelcey, & Dong, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">Raudenbush & Liu, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Murayama, Judd, & Sakaki, 2022)</ref>, they are limited insofar that they primarily apply to simplistic model specifications that are less complex than the models substantive researchers typically want to use, or they rely on using problematic test statistics <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Luke, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Because the issue of sample size requirements is not straightforward to address with analytic approaches, the field has relied heavily on simulation studies (Arnold, Hogan, Colford, & Hubbard, 2011).
text.formatted: Because the issue of sample size requirements is not straightforward to address with analytic approaches, the field has relied heavily on simulation studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Arnold, Hogan, Colford, & Hubbard, 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Perhaps the single most influential simulation study for multilevel sample size is Maas and Hox (2005).
text.formatted: Perhaps the single most influential simulation study for multilevel sample size is <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref>.

text.text: In their original study, the authors found that Level-2 sample sizes greater than 50 units tended to result in unbiased standard errors, and Level-2 sample sizes as small as 10 units tended to result in unbiased regression coefficients at both levels.
These findings have informed thousands of published research studies, as shown by its high citation count (over 4,550 times, according to an April, 2024 hierarchical data-pooling.
Google Scholar search).
In many scientific fields, potentially high impact research is subject to additional scrutiny and replication to ensure the veracity of its findings.

For example in the field of astronomy, a report claiming to discover phosphine in Venus' atmosphere, which could imply the presence of life, was immediately replicated by other independent teams and quickly debunked (Villanueva et al., 2021).
text.formatted: For example in the field of astronomy, a report claiming to discover phosphine in Venus' atmosphere, which could imply the presence of life, was immediately replicated by other independent teams and quickly debunked <ref type="bibr">(Villanueva et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Scholars acknowledge that not all studies need to be replicated, and that replications should not be done at random (Kuehberger & Schulte-Mecklenbeck, 2018).
text.formatted: Scholars acknowledge that not all studies need to be replicated, and that replications should not be done at random <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Kuehberger & Schulte-Mecklenbeck, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Rather, the potential and realized impact plays an important role in determining what to replicate (Witte & Zenker, 2018; Coles, Tiokhin, Scheel, Isager, & Lakens, 2018).
text.formatted: Rather, the potential and realized impact plays an important role in determining what to replicate <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Witte & Zenker, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Coles, Tiokhin, Scheel, Isager, & Lakens, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Indeed, recent attempts to replicate simulation studies focus on high citation count as criteria for inclusion (Luijken et al., 2024; Fairchild, Yin, Baraldi, Astivia, & Shi, 2024).
text.formatted: Indeed, recent attempts to replicate simulation studies focus on high citation count as criteria for inclusion <ref type="bibr">(Luijken et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fairchild, Yin, Baraldi, Astivia, & Shi, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The study by Maas and Hox (2005) is very highly cited, and, as will be demonstrated later, used to justify sample size for many substantive studies, meaning that this study has a core impact on a broad research literature.
text.formatted: The study by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> is very highly cited, and, as will be demonstrated later, used to justify sample size for many substantive studies, meaning that this study has a core impact on a broad research literature.

text.text: If its findings are not replicable, this could have a large impact on our trust in the citing literature and have practical implications for how multilevel sample size planning is conducted in the future.
While high impact studies are important to replicate, others have warned against committing additional resources to already precise findings (Singh Chawla, 2016).
text.formatted: While high impact studies are important to replicate, others have warned against committing additional resources to already precise findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Singh Chawla, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This is perhaps a reason why statistical simulation research has seen little scrutiny until recent years: the methods are often very precise, leaving little room for sampling variability as an explanation for failure to replicate.
However, this does not make simulations immune to a lack of replicability.

Recent examples of replications in simulations include a failure to replicate the oft cited "1 variable for 10 events" rule in logistic regression (van Smeden et al., 2016); by contrast, Fairchild et al. (2024) generally replicated the results of Curran, West, and Finch (1996) on the robustness of test statistics in confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to non-normal data, but this result did not generalize.
text.formatted: Recent examples of replications in simulations include a failure to replicate the oft cited "1 variable for 10 events" rule in logistic regression <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">(van Smeden et al., 2016)</ref>; by contrast, <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fairchild et al. (2024)</ref> generally replicated the results of <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Curran, West, and Finch (1996)</ref> on the robustness of test statistics in confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) to non-normal data, but this result did not generalize.

text.text: Replications are also often included either implicitly or explicitly as part of extensions of existing research (McNeish & Wolf, 2021; Montoya, 2022; Plantz, Brown, Wright, & Flake, 2024). Jelizarow, Guillemot, Tenenhaus, Strimmer, and Boulesteix (2010) demonstrated how different choices of conditions, datasets, and competing methods (i.e., simulator degrees of freedom) can be manipulated to demonstrate the superiority of a clearly inferior method.
text.formatted: Replications are also often included either implicitly or explicitly as part of extensions of existing research <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(McNeish & Wolf, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Montoya, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Plantz, Brown, Wright, & Flake, 2024)</ref>. <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Jelizarow, Guillemot, Tenenhaus, Strimmer, and Boulesteix (2010)</ref> demonstrated how different choices of conditions, datasets, and competing methods (i.e., simulator degrees of freedom) can be manipulated to demonstrate the superiority of a clearly inferior method.

text.text: Ultimately, this suggests that the replicability of simulation studies should not be taken as a certainty.

These issues have led to recent calls for more replication attempts of simulation studies (Boulesteix, Hoffman, Charlton, & Seibold, 2020; Rougier et al., 2017; Lohmann, Astivia, Morris, & Groenwold, 2022).
text.formatted: These issues have led to recent calls for more replication attempts of simulation studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Boulesteix, Hoffman, Charlton, & Seibold, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Rougier et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Lohmann, Astivia, Morris, & Groenwold, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: This burgeoning area of research has identified several reasons why simulation studies might be subject to the same replicability concerns as substantive empirical work.
First, simulation studies are just as subject to clerical errors as any scientific endeavor (Lohmann et al., 2022).
text.formatted: First, simulation studies are just as subject to clerical errors as any scientific endeavor <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Lohmann et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Even innocuous software bugs or coding errors can be enough to derail a simulation study.

Second, analytic flexibility can also apply to simulation studies in the form of selective or incomplete reporting, choosing random number generator seeds that produce outlier results ("seed hacking"), unclear decision boundaries about what constitutes model or method failure, and so on (Luijken et al., 2024; Jelizarow et al., 2010).
text.formatted: Second, analytic flexibility can also apply to simulation studies in the form of selective or incomplete reporting, choosing random number generator seeds that produce outlier results ("seed hacking"), unclear decision boundaries about what constitutes model or method failure, and so on <ref type="bibr">(Luijken et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Jelizarow et al., 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Third, descriptions of simulation studies may contain ambiguous information (Luijken et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Third, descriptions of simulation studies may contain ambiguous information <ref type="bibr">(Luijken et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: A study may inadvertently introduce ambiguity by using imprecise or flexible notation, omitting descriptions of intermediate steps, or providing contradicting information.
This fourth reason is particularly germane to the current replication, as we detail in the next section.
Collectively, these reasons underscore the growing need to replicate published simulation studies, particularly those of high impact and low precision.
A failure to replicate could help identify errors in the original simulation, software specific properties, and help to resolve ambiguities in the existing literature.
A successful replication may add to the existing evidence for a certain claim within the parameters of the specific study, but does not contribute to the claim's generalizability.
While replication is important for simulation studies, so too is generalizability.

Simulations are often conducted under limited conditions, and it is important to evaluate how generalizable the claims are to broader conditions. Fairchild et al. (2024) demonstrated how different methods for generating non-normal data provide different results with respect to robustness of CFA statistics.
text.formatted: Simulations are often conducted under limited conditions, and it is important to evaluate how generalizable the claims are to broader conditions. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Fairchild et al. (2024)</ref> demonstrated how different methods for generating non-normal data provide different results with respect to robustness of CFA statistics.

text.text: This result calls to question much of the existing literature on robustness to assumption violations, particularly in cases where there are multiple ways to simulate those violations.
The generalizability of Maas and Hox (2005) is important because the original study was simplistic.
text.formatted: The generalizability of <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> is important because the original study was simplistic.

text.text: This had the effect of leading substantive researchers to cite Maas and Hox (2005) in justification of modeling specifications and research designs that were never tested in the original study.
text.formatted: This had the effect of leading substantive researchers to cite <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> in justification of modeling specifications and research designs that were never tested in the original study.

text.text: While plenty of other simulation studies on multilevel sample size requirements were published after Maas and Hox (2005), their subsequent designs did not necessarily extend the complexity of model parameters that correspond to routine use cases encountered by substantive researchers (e.g., cases with more than one predictor at each level, testing a relatively restricted range of standardized effect sizes, etc.) (Arend & Schäfer, 2019; Lane & Hennes, 2018; Lafit, Adolf, Dejonckeere, Viechtbauer, & Ceulemans, 2021; Mathieu, Aguinis, Culpepper, & Chen, 2012).
text.formatted: While plenty of other simulation studies on multilevel sample size requirements were published after <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref>, their subsequent designs did not necessarily extend the complexity of model parameters that correspond to routine use cases encountered by substantive researchers (e.g., cases with more than one predictor at each level, testing a relatively restricted range of standardized effect sizes, etc.) <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Arend & Schäfer, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">Lane & Hennes, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Lafit, Adolf, Dejonckeere, Viechtbauer, & Ceulemans, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Mathieu, Aguinis, Culpepper, & Chen, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: These studies focus on cases with only one predictor at each level, or probe needed sample sizes for highly specialized use cases (e.g., dyadic models, intensive longitudinal studies).
This begs the question: Does the original recommendation of 50 Level-2 units and 10 Level-1 units generalize to more complex use cases?

To put this point differently, the field's enthusiasm for multilevel modeling has resulted in the implementation of increasingly complex modeling cases, yet collective interest in verifying whether foundational research on sample size sufficiency generalizes to such cases is only starting to emerge (Enders, Keller, & Woller, 2023).

text.text: In response to these issues, this registered report presents a replication of Maas and Hox (2005) and proposes an extension of their original study driven by trends in research papers that have recently cited it.

text.text: We also encourage better adoption of established reporting guidelines for multilevel analyses aimed at enhancing scholarly communication about model specification, as this issue is critical to the current study.

The following sections review the original specifications of Maas and Hox (2005) and their results, present the results of our replication simulation study, describe findings from a brief survey of substantive literature citing the original simulation, and summarize our proposed extension.

text.text: Equation 3 is a two-level model with one Level-1 predictor (X ij ), and one Level-2 predictor Z j .
The coefficients correspond to a fixed effect intercept (γ 00 ), the fixed effect of the Level-1 predictor (γ 01 ), the effect of the Level-2 predictor (γ 10 ), and a cross-level interaction (γ 11 ).
This model allows for variation among higher-level units in both the means of Y ij (u 0j ) as well as the within-unit effect of X ij (u 1j ).
The difference between fitted and observed Y ij values, e ij , is assumed to be normally distributed with expectation zero, variance σ 2 e and independent of random effects.
Assumptions about residuals from the empty model described above apply here.
X ij , Z j , and X ij Z j are uncorrelated based on the way the data were generated.

One way in which this manifests is a lack of clarity regarding the precise ICC quantity used to simulate data.

There are two common ICCs used in the multilevel literature: the total ICC (typically just referred to as ICC) presented in Equation 2 and the residual ICC (rICC) which replaces the values in Equation 2 with values from a model with predictors (here notated using quantities without asterisks).

The original article does not differentiate between the unconditional quantities τ * 00 and σ 2 * e introduced in Equation 2 from τ 00 and σ 2 e , which describe the variance of u 0j and e ij in Equation 3; rather, they use the same symbols for both quantities.
This is a subtle yet critical distinction because τ * 00 and σ 2 * e define measures of total variation whereas τ 00 and σ 2 e represent measures of residual variance from the focal simulation model.
This distinction is not mentioned in Maas and Hox (2005), and the authors go on to use these two quantities interchangeably.

Assuming the original authors intended to use ρ res , the original simulation employed a fully crossed 3 x 3 x 3 factorial design in which they varied the rICC (ρ res = {0.1, 0.2, 0.3}), Level-2 sample size (N = {30, 50, 100}), and Level-1 sample size (n = {5, 30, 50}).

Restricted Maximum Likelihood Estimation (RML) in MLwiN.
X ij and Z j values were originally generated from a standard normal distribution for the smallest cell size (N = 30, n = 5) and were 'repeated' for conditions with larger sample sizes.

text.text: Unfortunately the original article did not report the average parameter estimates, so it is not possible to confirm our assumptions about the values of τ 00 from their simulation results.

The primary outcome of the study was percent relative bias, a metric of parameter estimate accuracy, given by 100 × ( θ -θ) / θ, such that θ is the population parameter and θ is the average observed parameter estimate.

Confidence interval (CI) accuracy (95%) was analyzed by examining each interval's non-coverage for all parameters (regression coefficients, variance components, and Level-1 variance). Maas and Hox (2005) conducted a series of logistic regressions to determine whether a given factor (rICC, Level-1 sample size, Level-2 sample size) predicted CI non-coverage, using an α threshold of .01 for significance.

text.text: The results of the study showed negligible bias across regression coefficients, having an average of 0.05%, with the greatest relative bias overall in the condition with the smallest sample sizes and largest rICC (0.3).

With respect to non-coverage, the authors found that the Level-2 sample size influenced non-coverage of the variance components (T), intercept (γ 00 ), and the coefficient for X ij (γ 10 ), with the non-coverage rates being higher for the variance components (approx. 8%) compared to the fixed effects (approx.
A similar pattern was observed for Level-1 sample size, such that varying the sample size more drastically affected variance components than regression coefficients.

The same pattern was observed with respect to rICC, as varying the Level-2 sample size affected the variance components (T) but not the fixed effect regression coefficients (γ 00 , γ 01 , γ 10 , γ 11 ).
Fixed effect regression coefficients and Level-1 error (σ 2 e ) had non-coverage rates comparable to the nominal non-coverage rate (5%-6%) across the other conditions.

From these results, Maas and Hox (2005) conclude that a small Level-2 sample size (equal to or less than 50) lead to biased Level-2 standard errors (e.g., non-coverage rates on parameters decreased as sample sizes increased); the authors deemed non-coverage rates around 7% with 50 units was acceptable in practice.

text.text: The authors reported that all 27,000 fitted models converged.
When simulating data and fitting this model, Maas and Hox (2005) made several notable assumptions and analytic choices that limit the original study's generalizability.
text.formatted: When simulating data and fitting this model, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> made several notable assumptions and analytic choices that limit the original study's generalizability.

text.text: We focus on four major limitations of the original simulation.

First, the model presented in Equation 3 was the only model in the simulation, meaning the effect of adding additional predictors (at either level) and cross-level interactions on sample size requirements cannot be inferred from the results of their simulation study.
Second, the original study assumed perfectly balanced sample sizes across all Level-2 units (i.e., all Level-2 units shared the same number of Level-1 units nested within them).
Third, they assumed no covariance between random effects (i.e., τ01 = 0) when simulating the datafoot_1 .
text.formatted: Third, they assumed no covariance between random effects (i.e., τ01 = 0) when simulating the data<ref type="foot" target="#foot_1">foot_1</ref> .

text.text: Fourth, they also assumed the random effects variances for the random slopes and intercepts were identical, τ00 = τ 11 .

These latter three assumptions are rarely satisfied in practice -Level-2 units are routinely imbalanced, random effects tend to covary to a non-zero degree, and random variances are almost never equal (Enders et al., 2023).
text.formatted: These latter three assumptions are rarely satisfied in practice -Level-2 units are routinely imbalanced, random effects tend to covary to a non-zero degree, and random variances are almost never equal <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Enders et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: While these simplifying assumptions were necessary as a first step when the original study was conducted, the consequence of violating them is unknown but will be explored in our extensions of the simulation after our replication.
Here we present our replication of Maas and Hox (2005), following their original simulation procedures as closely as possible.
text.formatted: Here we present our replication of <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref>, following their original simulation procedures as closely as possible.

text.text: Our goal in conducting the replication was to confirm or dispute the original study's recommendation that N = 50 is needed for sufficiently estimating parameters and standard errors without bias.
In practice, this meant that we were looking to observe the same conditions that led the original authors to make that recommendation.

This meant that in a successful replication (i) the bias of all model parameters did not exceed 5%foot_2 and (ii) non-coverage rates did not vary significantly as a function of condition or, if they were significant, exhibited a non-coverage rate below 7.5%.

One potential deviation from the original study, and another point of ambiguity, concerns the data simulation procedure.
The authors' noted that data were simulated for the smallest possible Level-1 and Level-2 sample size combination and then duplicated for larger combinations.
It was unclear how this duplication was conducted.
In our replication, we duplicated the initial data from the smallest combination however many times needed to achieve a larger sample size.
In the event that duplicating the initial dataset exceeded the desired sample size, the final copy of the initial dataset was truncated.
We fitted the multilevel models in this study using the lme4 package in R using REML (Bates, Mächler, Bolker, & Walker, 2015).

Notably, lme4 does not offer Wald confidence intervals for the variance components.
In order to be consistent with the original study, we wrote custom code to compute the necessary statistics.
Results are reported below.
Relative bias is reported first, followed by non-coverage.
Methods for analyzing each outcome are detailed in the respective subsections.
Relative Bias.
Results for relative bias are listed in the Appendix (Supplementary Tables 1 2 3).
text.formatted: Results for relative bias are listed in the Appendix (Supplementary Tables <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref> <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref> <ref type="table" target="#tab_2">3</ref>).

text.text: Bias was low across the board for all parameters.

Because bias values in these conditions were less than 10% (the largest cell among them was 5.9% for random slope variance in the n = 5 level, though all but eight values fell below 1%), we conclude that the original results replicate with respect to relative bias and these particular parameters.
Coverage.
We created an indicator variable for each parameter within each replicated dataset to code for whether the 95% confidence intervals included the true parameter (1 = non-coverage,0 = coverage).

To produce a table of results aligned with the original study, we regressed these indicator values over a given condition of interest (Level-2 sample size, Level-1 sample size, or ICC) for each parameter in the simulation.
This resulted in 21 separate logistic regressions with each model corresponding to one condition and one parameter (3 conditions x 7 parameters).
Within each regression the levels of the predictor variable were entered as two dummy codes.

We then conducted a likelihood ratio test of the full model containing the dummy codes compared to the null model to determine whether adding the codes (corresponding to a simulation condition) to the model explained more variability than would be expected under the null.
For consistency with the original simulation, we adopted an alpha threshold of 0.01.

Table 1 lists the non-coverage of 95% confidence intervals of each model parameter estimate by the number of units, Table 2 lists non-coverage of parameter estimates by unit size, and Table 3 lists non-coverage of parameter estimates by rICC values.
Non-coverage rates in our replication were broadly comparable to those reported in Maas and Hox (2005).
text.formatted: Non-coverage rates in our replication were broadly comparable to those reported in <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref>.

text.text: We did observe some slight deviations.
First, non-coverage rates across the board were generally lower.

Second, the results of a few significance tests (i.e., reject or fail to reject the null hypothesis that a given condition had no effect on non-coverage for a given parameter) were different than the original study.
However, even in these cases, non-coverage values were still quite low (slightly lower than observed in the original study) such that it would likely not make a practical difference.
While the original authors did not examine interactions between conditions, these interactions may exist.
Mimicking the analytical process in our extension (see below), we tested for interactions in the non-coverage replication simulation data.
We did so by first testing for the significance of the highest order (three-way) interaction and then iteratively tested all possible lower order (two-way) interactions for all parameter estimates.
We observed no significant three-way or subsequent two-way interactions for the intercept (γ 00 ), slopes (γ 01 , γ 10 , γ 11 ), and Level-1 error variance (σ 2 e ).
We first observed a significant three-way interaction between rICC, N (number of groups) and n (group size) for the random slope variance (τ 10 , p = 0.003).
Unpacking this three-way interaction revealed significant two-way interactions between N and n at two levels of rICC.
First, when rICC = 0.1 and n = 5 (p = 0.008) non-coverage decreases with increasing N , but not at other levels of n (n = 30, p > 0.250; n = 50, p > 0.250).

text.text: Non-coverage rates decrease with increasing n at all levels of N but more so at higher N (N = 30, p < .001; N = 50, p = 0.002; N = 100, p < .001).

text.text: When rICC = 0.2, there was a significant interaction between n and N (p = .002) such that standard error bias increases with N when n = 5 (p = .003), but less so at other levels of n (n = 30, p = 0.050; n = 50, p > 0.250).

text.text: Non-coverage decreases with changes in n when N = 30 (p < 0.001) but not when N = 50 (p = 0.072) or N = 100 (p > 0.250).

text.text: When rICC = 0.3, there was not a significant two-way interaction between n and N (p = 0.232) and the simple effects show no significant effects of n on non-coverage at any level of N , nor any significant effects of N at any level of n (p-values ranging between 0.043 and 0.977).

Looking at the interaction another way, there is a significant two-way interaction between N and rICC when n = 5 (p = 0.001), such that non-coverage decreased with larger N when rICC = 0.1 (p = 0.004) but increased with larger N when rICC = 0.2 (no significant simple slope found when rICC = 0.3, p = 0.044).
Non-coverage increased with larger rICC values across levels of N (N = 30, p = 0.009; N = 50, p < 0.001; N = 100, p < 0.001).

text.text: Finally, when N = 100 we observed a significant interaction between n and rICC (p < 0.001).

text.text: Non-coverage increased with n when rICC = 0.1 (p < 0.001) but not when rICC = 0.2 (p > 0.250) or 0.3 (p = 0.118), and it increased with rICC when n = 5 (p < 0.001) but not when n = 30 (p > 0.250) or 50 (p > 0.250).

text.text: Next, we observed a significant two-way interaction between rICC and n for the random intercept (τ 00 ) parameter (p = 0.001).

Unpacking this interaction revealed significant effects of rICC on non-coverage rates when n = 5 (p < 0.001), and of n on standard error bias when rICC was equal to 0.1 (p < 0.001) and 0.2 (p = 0.002).

text.text: In all cases, bias increased with increases in the focal predictor (rICC or n).
Non-coverage rates for all cells in these interactions were all below 7.5%.

text.text: These analyses provide a template for how interaction effects will be interrogated in the extension simulation.
Code for these analyses is available on our OSF repository.

We generally replicated the results of the original simulation, confirming the authors' conclusion that achieving acceptably low bias and non-coverage in the model requires Level-2 sample sizes of at least N = 50.
In fact, this replication shows that some of the non-coverage rates in the original study were perhaps slightly inflated.

We are encouraged by the relatively high rate of replication across model parameters with respect to non-coverage as well as the fact that most of the non-replications indicated less non-coverage than before.
We take this to be good news for studies in the last twenty years that have relied on the guidelines initially proffered by Maas and Hox (2005).
text.formatted: We take this to be good news for studies in the last twenty years that have relied on the guidelines initially proffered by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref>.

text.text: While it is encouraging the findings from Maas and Hox (2005) replicated, it is important to contextualize how other researchers cite the original study in the broader literature.
text.formatted: While it is encouraging the findings from <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> replicated, it is important to contextualize how other researchers cite the original study in the broader literature.

text.text: Simulation studies are only informative to the extent that substantive researchers do not deviate too far from the original conditions of the simulation.
Extrapolating from these conditions does not guarantee comparable model performance.
To that point, little is known about how other researchers use Maas and Hox (2005) to justify their research designs.
text.formatted: To that point, little is known about how other researchers use <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> to justify their research designs.

text.text: This is critical to know because it is unclear whether the main recommendation by the authors would hold up under more realistic data structures and more complicated models encountered in modern research settings.
In response to this, we surveyed recently published literature to motivate and inform the proposed extension of the original study.
We conducted a survey of 50 journal articles reporting substantive empirical reports between 2018 and 2022 to determine how scholars have been citing Maas and Hox (2005) in their own work.
text.formatted: We conducted a survey of 50 journal articles reporting substantive empirical reports between 2018 and 2022 to determine how scholars have been citing <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> in their own work.

text.text: All papers examined were published in peer-reviewed journals spanning several fields (psychology, neuroscience, political science, marketing, nursing, etc.), mostly within the social and biomedical sciences.
Peer-review articles for the survey were identified by using Google Scholar's interface to retrieve papers that cited the original study and were published in the aforementioned time frame.
The search returned 2,490 articles.
Papers were selected at random from the list returned by Google Scholar.
Review articles or papers on quantitative methods research were excluded such that they were screened out of sample papers and then replaced with a new one from the population.

The following 11 items of information were extracted from each paper to evaluate how Maas and Hox (2005) is being cited: (1) reason for citing, (2) Level-1 sample sizefoot_3 , (3) whether there were imbalanced units, (4) Level-2 sample size, (5) number of random effects (including random intercepts), (6) number of Level-1 fixed effect regression coefficients (excluding intercepts), (7) number of Level-2 regression coefficients (excluding intercepts), (8) number of cross-level interactions, (9) ICC, (10) whether the authors reported random effect covariance (if applicable), (11) any other noteworthy information (e.g., if they specified a multilevel structural equation model, if they used multilevel logistic regression, if a three-level model was specified, etc.).
text.formatted: The following 11 items of information were extracted from each paper to evaluate how Maas and Hox (2005) is being cited: (1) reason for citing, (2) Level-1 sample size<ref type="foot" target="#foot_3">foot_3</ref> , (3) whether there were imbalanced units, (4) Level-2 sample size, (5) number of random effects (including random intercepts), (6) number of Level-1 fixed effect regression coefficients (excluding intercepts), (7) number of Level-2 regression coefficients (excluding intercepts), (8) number of cross-level interactions, (9) ICC, (10) whether the authors reported random effect covariance (if applicable), (11) any other noteworthy information (e.g., if they specified a multilevel structural equation model, if they used multilevel logistic regression, if a three-level model was specified, etc.).

text.text: The spreadsheet summarizing these findings can be accessed on our OSF page.
Two coders (JB, AC) independently evaluated the journal articles according to the 11 items listed above.
If information was unavailable, the field was marked as missing.
The two coders met approximately on a weekly basis with the first author to resolve disagreements in the coding.
Disagreements were resolved by returning to the given article, evaluating the information as a group, and achieving unanimous consensus.
The most common disagreements were when one coder did not find relevant information, and so listed a field as "missing" whereas the other coder found the information.
A summary of journals and articles represented in our literature search, aggregated by field, is displayed in Supplementary Table 4 (Appendix).
A disaggregated list can be accessed on our OSF page.
The majority of authors cite Maas and Hox (2005) to justify their sample size (most frequently Level-2, 44% of studies explicitly citing for Level-2 sample size).
text.formatted: The majority of authors cite <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> to justify their sample size (most frequently Level-2, 44% of studies explicitly citing for Level-2 sample size).

text.text: Alarmingly, a notable subset (8%) of them miscite the paper in some way (e.g., claiming a smaller sample size is acceptable than what was originally reported, justifying a drastically different type of model like a three-level model, etc.).
Other reasons for citing Maas and Hox (2005) were to justify the general use of a multilevel model, or justify not using a three-level model.
text.formatted: Other reasons for citing <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> were to justify the general use of a multilevel model, or justify not using a three-level model.

text.text: In terms of Level-1 sample size, 26%, 66%, and 72% of studies reported Level-1 sample sizes below n = 5, 30, and 50, respectively.

These values correspond to the three levels of n included in the original simulation; we present these as benchmarks since Maas and Hox (2005) did not make strong or explicit recommendations about Level-1 sample size. 0%, 10%, and 48% report Level-2 sample sizes below N = 30, 50, and 100, respectively.
text.formatted: These values correspond to the three levels of n included in the original simulation; we present these as benchmarks since <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> did not make strong or explicit recommendations about Level-1 sample size. 0%, 10%, and 48% report Level-2 sample sizes below N = 30, 50, and 100, respectively.

text.text: Notably, 88% report imbalanced Level-1 sample sizes across Level-2 units (6% report balance; 6% were unclear).
Only 46% of papers surveyed reported an ICC, and of those reported, the range was .01 -.83 (0.32 mean, 0.26 median), exceeding the range examined in the original Maas and Hox (2005) report.
text.formatted: Only 46% of papers surveyed reported an ICC, and of those reported, the range was .01 -.83 (0.32 mean, 0.26 median), exceeding the range examined in the original <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> report.

text.text: This wide range of ICC values is consistent with meta-analyses of various subfields (Glassman, Potter, Baumler, & Coyle, 2015; Bolger & Laurenceau, 2013; Arend & Schäfer, 2019), many of which were published after the original report.

text.text: Of the papers reporting an intraclass correlation coefficient, 47.82% did not clearly designate whether they used the null ICC or the rICC, 43.48% reported the null ICC, and 8.70% reported both quantities.
The majority of published studies ran models that were more complex than Maas and Hox (2005).
text.formatted: The majority of published studies ran models that were more complex than <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref>.

text.text: Seventy-four percent included more than one Level-1 predictor, 66% included more than one Level-2 predictor, and 30% included more than one cross-level interaction.
Nineteen percent of studies reported running models with more than two random effects.

Only three papers reported the covariance between random effects when applicable-in fact, most papers did not even specify whether they constrained these parameters to zero or whether they let it vary freely.
Anecdotally, several papers provided an impoverished account of the models they were specifying.
It was difficult to identify basic information in several papers, such as the number of predictors at either level, number of random slopes, and even, in some cases, the sample size.

text.text: This review suggests the modern multilevel modeling studies have exceeded the complexity of the initial simulations conducted to inform them.

Although this is typically a hallmark of scientific progress, enthusiasm for more involved modeling has ostensibly outstripped the guidelines that substantive researchers actively use to plan and justify their study designs.

This is in spite of subsequent work that advanced our understanding of sample size planning for multilevel modeling studies, such as by providing closed-form solutions for simplistic models or simulations for special modeling cases (e.g., logistic regression, variable skew) (Westfall et al., 2014; Astivia, Gadermann, & Guhn, 2019; Judd, Westfall, & Kenny, 2017; Mathieu et al., 2012; Murayama et al., 2022).
text.formatted: This is in spite of subsequent work that advanced our understanding of sample size planning for multilevel modeling studies, such as by providing closed-form solutions for simplistic models or simulations for special modeling cases (e.g., logistic regression, variable skew) <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Westfall et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">Astivia, Gadermann, & Guhn, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Judd, Westfall, & Kenny, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Mathieu et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Murayama et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: While these aforementioned studies have received considerable attention in their own right, we believe the continued reliance on Maas and Hox (2005) is centered on the fact that more work is needed to align simulation studies of multilevel sample size with common practice.

text.text: Overview.
In response to our replication findings and the literature survey, we proposed four extensions to the original Maas and Hox (2005) simulation.
text.formatted: In response to our replication findings and the literature survey, we proposed four extensions to the original <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> simulation.

text.text: We briefly introduce these extensions here and then detail their implementation in the context of the broader simulation procedure below.
First, we varied the number of Level-1 slopes and cross-level interactions.

Second, we derived the population parameters in a different way than the original authors (Enders et al., 2023; Rights & Sterba, 2019), opting to simulate data and subsequently model coefficients in terms of the total variance explained by various parts of the model (e.g., within-unit predictors, cross-level interactions, etc.).
text.formatted: Second, we derived the population parameters in a different way than the original authors <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Enders et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Rights & Sterba, 2019)</ref>, opting to simulate data and subsequently model coefficients in terms of the total variance explained by various parts of the model (e.g., within-unit predictors, cross-level interactions, etc.).

text.text: Third, we added levels with unbalanced Level-1 units (i.e., the value of n varies across Level-2 units).
Fourth, and last, we used the total ICC (i.e., ρ * ) to simulate data (instead of the rICC) and added an additional ICC value (0.4) to better reflect results from our literature survey.

For the sake of transparency, we note here that we initially wanted to include a condition that tested how the correlation between random effects impacted bias and coverage, but we decided to not pursue this because there was not enough information in the published literature to identify values for such a condition and also because others suggest that fixed effect coefficients are not sensitive to these covariances (Snijders & Bosker, 2012).
text.formatted: For the sake of transparency, we note here that we initially wanted to include a condition that tested how the correlation between random effects impacted bias and coverage, but we decided to not pursue this because there was not enough information in the published literature to identify values for such a condition and also because others suggest that fixed effect coefficients are not sensitive to these covariances <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Snijders & Bosker, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Our simulation used three two-level models, constituting the first proposed extension.
In addition to the original two-level model from Equation (3), the following two models were included.
The model in equation 10 has two Level-1 predictors and two cross-level interactions.
The model in equation 11 has three Level-1 predictors and three cross-level interactions.
Note that a numeral has been added to the X variables to differentiate between Level-1 predictors.
We used a different data generation mechanism for the proposed extension, representing our second proposed extension.

Previously, Maas and Hox (2005) simulated X and Z data from standard normal distributions with a sample size corresponding to the smallest combination of N and n and 'repeated' rows if necessary for larger sample size combinations.
text.formatted: Previously, <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> simulated X and Z data from standard normal distributions with a sample size corresponding to the smallest combination of N and n and 'repeated' rows if necessary for larger sample size combinations.

text.text: They then generated the stochastic components of the slope and intercept, used the full model coefficients to compute E(Y |X, Z, u), and then added residuals.
Here we took a different approach by deriving the population parameters based on percent variance explained by the model terms (Rights & Sterba, 2019).
text.formatted: Here we took a different approach by deriving the population parameters based on percent variance explained by the model terms <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Rights & Sterba, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, instead of setting population parameters and then generating data, we set the percent variance explained by each model component, derived population parameters, and then simulated data.
This procedure involved specifying the percentage of variance explained by various sources: within-unit predictors, between-unit predictors, cross-level interactions, and random slopes.
Two additional sources of variance-random intercept variance and Level-1 residual variance-are obtained by subtraction.
The percent variances explained by the model components are used to systematically reverse engineer model coefficients and variance components.
Finally, we note that we did not repeat, or 'stack' rows in our design matrix as the original study.

We planned to test the following three different combinations of percent variance explained proportions by Level-1, Level-2, and cross-level fixed effect terms: (Level-1 -0.095, Level-2 -0.095, cross-level -0.095; Level-1 -0.065, Level-2 -0.065, cross-level -0.025;
Level-1 -0.035, Level-2 -0.035, cross-level -0.01).
Proportion variance explained by random slopes was held at 0.1 across all levels of this condition.

In models with more than one predictor, the percent variance was partitioned across the predictors such that the total percent variance explained for each set of predictors (Level-1, Level-2, cross-level) was distributed equally across predictors.
Each set of values assumed an outcome variable with a mean of 1.
The first set of values were specified to approximate the initial model coefficients specified by Maas and Hox (2005).
text.formatted: The first set of values were specified to approximate the initial model coefficients specified by <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref>.

text.text: The latter two sets reflect realistic values observed in the literature (Rights & Sterba, 2019).
text.formatted: The latter two sets reflect realistic values observed in the literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Rights & Sterba, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Functionalities of the mlmpower package (Enders et al., 2023) were used to calculate model coefficients and simulate data.
text.formatted: Functionalities of the mlmpower package <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Enders et al., 2023)</ref> were used to calculate model coefficients and simulate data.

text.text: The Level-1 predictors were generated with a population ICC of zero, such that there was no systematic between-cluster variability in the predictors.
Cluster means therefore varied across clusters by chance, meaning that observed ICC values of the Level-1 predictors were close to, but not exactly, zerofoot_4 .
text.formatted: Cluster means therefore varied across clusters by chance, meaning that observed ICC values of the Level-1 predictors were close to, but not exactly, zero<ref type="foot" target="#foot_4">foot_4</ref> .

text.text: Note that in other contexts, one would need to also be mindful of the means and variances of cross-product terms; here the means and variances are equal to 0 and 1, respectively, because of our particular centering choices, but it would otherwise depend on the scaling of the factors comprising the product terms and the ICCs of the Level-1 terms.

Consequently, because the Level-1 and Level-2 predictors had zero means and were uncorrelated with one another owing to the Level-1 predictors having an ICC of zero, the percent variance explained from each model component (Level-1 slopes, Level-2 slopes, cross-level interactions) was additive.

Finally, for the sake of comparison, it is worth noting that based on the model coefficients and random effects variances of the original study, the proportion variance explained by the Level-1 and cross-level interaction (centering within groups effectively turns the cross-level interaction into a Level-1 slope, for variance partitioning purposes) ranged from 13 to 19%, whereas the proportion variance explained by the Level-2 slopes ranged from 6 to 10%.
Data were simulated to include different degrees of imbalance between Level-1 predictors, representing our third proposed extension.
Specifically, we added levels 7 with unbalanced cases such that the sample size ratio between the largest unit size and smallest unit size varied from 1:1, 1.5:1, 2:1, and 2.5:1.
text.formatted: Specifically, we added levels <ref type="foot" target="#foot_5">7</ref> with unbalanced cases such that the sample size ratio between the largest unit size and smallest unit size varied from 1:1, 1.5:1, 2:1, and 2.5:1.

text.text: The center of the range of Level-1 group sizes corresponds to the average Level-1 group size level, corresponding to the ideal value given no imbalance (5, 30, or 50).
Arithmetic is then used to solve for the minimum and maximum sample size.

For example, if the average group size 30 and the ratio is 2:1 then the minimum was 20 and the max was 30 (some ratios result in non-whole numbers, so these numbers are rounded to the closest whole number prior to data generation).
Level-1 group sizes (n) for a given simulated dataset were drawn from a uniform distribution.
The lower bound of the distribution's range corresponded to the minimum sample size and the upper bound corresponded to a maximum sample size.
Finally, data generation included an additional level for the ICC (0.4) in line with the results from our literature survey.
This constitutes the fourth and final proposed extension of the original simulation.
Given these four extensions and their respective levels (summarized in Table 5), the proposed extension was intended to comprise 3,888 unique conditions.
text.formatted: Given these four extensions and their respective levels (summarized in Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_4">5</ref>), the proposed extension was intended to comprise 3,888 unique conditions.

text.text: The extension was designed to employ a comparable procedure as the original study and our replication.

A unique dataset was simulated within each cell (1,000/cell), lme4 fit the relevant model to the data using RML, and the statistical quantities of interest were extracted (parameter estimates, confidence intervals).
We proposed to analyze percent relative bias by examining the degree of bias in each level within each condition while collapsing across all other conditions.
If bias exceeded 5% but was less than 10%, we proposed to perform a one-sample t-test to determine whether the bias is significantly different from zero.

If levels within a condition were found to be significantly different from zero, we planned to perform a between-samples t-test for all pairwise levels within the same condition to determine whether they are significantly different from each other.
If bias exceeded 10%, we planned to simply conclude the degree of bias is unacceptably high.

We planned to analyze non-coverage rates by creating an indicator variable for non-coverage (1: 95% CI did not contain the parameter value, 0: it did) and then regressing these indicator values on the simulation conditions (consistent with the analysis of the original simulation).
This was intended to be an iterative process whereby all possible higher order interactions were to be tested, beginning with an interaction between all conditions.
If the highest order interaction(s) was not significant, we would drop to the next highest order interaction(s) until a model with no interactions was tested.
If any interaction was significant, we intended to test for simple slope significance for the lower order terms comprising the interaction.
If the interaction comprised three or more terms, then this would proceed in an iterative fashion.
These tests were intended help us determine whether non-coverage rates vary as a function of a given condition, or interactions between conditions.

text.text: The extension simulation explored how more realistic and complex multilevel model specifications-motivated by common practices in the current literature-impact relative bias and confidence interval coverage across a range of conditions.

We manipulated the number of Level-1 slopes and cross-level interactions ('Model Type'), the degree of imbalance in Level-1 sample sizes ('Imbalance'), the percentage of variance explained by fixed effects ('Variance Explained'), the total ICC ('ICC'), as well as both the Level-1 ('n') and Level-2 ('N') sample sizes.
In sum, the simulation was meant to comprise 1,296 conditions across three model specifications (3,888 total), with 1,000 replications per condition.

The following results section details deviations from our pre-planned analyses and then breaks down the results in terms of (i) percent relative bias of parameter estimates and (ii) non-coverage of 95% CIs.
Notably, although our simulation was initially meant to comprise 3,888 conditions in total, upon running the simulation we discovered unforeseen model identification issues.
Specifically, models that include more than one Level-1 predictor and cross-level interaction at the lowest Level-1 sample size (n) and with any imbalance could not be estimated.
This forced us to drop 864 conditions from the simulation.
We decided a priori to analyze relative bias by flagging values exceeding 5% and conducting a statistical test to determine if those rates differed from zero.
However, this analysis plan proved to be problematic to implement.

When planning, we inadvertently overlooked the fact that the disaggregated data comprises over 2,500,000 unique cases, which virtually guarantees that any statistical tests for cells exceeding the relative percent bias threshold of 5% would be statistically significant.
In our view, this obviates the utility of significance testing, which does not provide any additional meaningful information beyond plots and figures of relative bias rates.
In response to this, we opted to plot and table percent relative bias rates and highlight cells that are particularly high.
Relative bias values for unique simulation cells are depicted in Figures 5 6 7.

text.text: Notably, bias was observed to be close to zero for most cells involving γ 00 and γ 01 , and was within the nominal 5% cut-off for all other slope parameters.
Level-1 error variance (σ 2 e ) showed minimal bias across conditions.
The range of values is lengthened for models that are more complex (Figure 6), those that include more than three fixed effect terms.

text.text: However, the worst bias was observed in the variance components, specifically the random effect variances (Figure 7).
text.formatted: However, the worst bias was observed in the variance components, specifically the random effect variances (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_6">7</ref>).

text.text: Bias for τ 00 was exceedingly high in conditions marked by low ICC values (i.e., ICC = 0.1), particularly when the variance explained by fixed effects is high.
Moreover, τ 00 and the rest of the random slope variances showed extremely high biases in conditions where the Level-1 sample sizes were lowest (equal to n = 5).
Model parameters were somewhat robust to imbalanced cases, with modest (less than 5%) increases in relative bias observed between the highest and lowest imbalance conditions for most parameters.
One exception was the τ 11 and τ 33 parameters, which showed greater bias in highly imbalanced designs (and the parameter τ²2 to a lesser extent).
A subset of percent-relative bias rates from the most relevant conditions are reported in Table 6.

text.text: Initially, we had decided a priori to analyze non-coverage outcomes by regressing them on the simulation conditions using logistic regression and stepwise model comparison approach where the highest possible order interaction would be tested and then dropped iteratively as needed.
However, this too proved to be problematic.

Specifically, the large number of cases drastically inflated the computational cost of analyses when considering the proposed stepwise approach and that each of the study variables were factors comprised of several levels.

While we did indeed attempt to run the analyses we originally specified, the memory costs of fitting the models outstripped what was available to us (high performance computing cluster at the university) and prevented us from analyzing anything greater than a three-way interaction.

We proceeded with analyzing all possible three-way interactions for each parameter of interest, however most of these interactions and ensuing lower order (two-way) interactions were significant in a manner that was unwieldy for interpretation.
Specifically, the volume of significant interactions was sufficiently high and results were diffuse enough that it was conceptually challenging to interpret the results in a meaningful way.

To address this, we only examined main effects across all parameters while also plotting and tabling non-coverage statistics to show visual information about the interactions while also identifying individual cells that are particularly high.
Rates of non-coverage for select conditions are shown in Table 7; results for quantitative analyses of non-coverage are presented in Tables 8 -10 and visualized in Figures 8 -10.
text.formatted: Rates of non-coverage for select conditions are shown in Table <ref type="table">7</ref>; results for quantitative analyses of non-coverage are presented in Tables 8 -10 and visualized in Figures 8 -10.

text.text: In terms of fixed effects, the γ 10 and γ 11 parameters were most susceptible to high non-coverage across several simulation conditions, usually those involving high imbalance or smaller Level-1 sample sizes.
Other fixed effects were less susceptible, with the γ 30 parameter not showing any significant main effects.
Notably, the variance explained condition had a significant main effect on non-coverage for all cross-level interactions (Table 10).
text.formatted: Notably, the variance explained condition had a significant main effect on non-coverage for all cross-level interactions (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_7">10</ref>).

text.text: However, visual inspection of non-coverage rates show modest and inconsistent differences between conditions, suggesting that the observed effects were driven by the high sample size (i.e., number of unique conditions in a given analysis) and by rates that only slightly exceed the nominal 5% convention in the field of psychology (up to 7 or 8%).
By contrast, the variance components showed differential levels of non-coverage, primarily depending on the specific type of parameter.
Specifically, the random slope variances were overwhelmingly prone to high non-coverage.

The Level-1 error variance (σ 2 e ) was most susceptible to non-coverage when the Level-1 sample sizes were low (n = 5), and the random intercept (τ 10 ) was prone to high non-coverage when the ICC was low (0.1) for models where the set of fixed effects explain relatively higher proportion of variance, as well as in models where the ICC and Level-1 sample size are low.
There is however again a disconnect between the quantitative results and the visualizations of the individual condition cells.
For instance, Table 10 shows significant main effects of all conditions on Level-1 error variance, but the plots did not indicate any stark apparent differences between cells.
