text.text: Taken together, the extension results reveal a clear divide between fixed effects and variance components.
Fixed effect estimates remained largely unbiased across conditions, even as model complexity increased, though modest elevations appeared in the most complex specifications.

Variance components were far more fragile: the random intercept variance showed pronounced bias under low ICC conditions, random slope variances were severely biased when Level-1 sample sizes were small, and imbalance amplified these problems.

Confidence interval coverage followed the same pattern, with acceptable coverage for variance components generally requiring at least Level-2 and Level-1 sample sizes in excess of 100 and 5, respectively.
The present study replicated and extended Maas and Hox's (2005) influential simulation on sample size requirements for multilevel models.
text.formatted: The present study replicated and extended <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox's (2005)</ref> influential simulation on sample size requirements for multilevel models.

text.text: We replicated their core findings: relative bias for fixed effects was negligible across most conditions, and the largest threats to coverage were observed for variance components, particularly random slope variances, when the number of Level-2 units was small.

These results reinforce the original recommendation that Level-2 sample sizes of at least 50 are generally needed to obtain unbiased parameter estimates for variance components, but suggest that accurate confidence intervals require larger sample sizes (in excess of N = 100).
Our extension addressed two broad gaps in the original work: the use of more Relative Bias.
Across the extended design, relative bias remained close to zero for most Level-1 and Level-2 fixed effects.

While bias was slightly elevated in various instances involving more complex models (e.g., those with more than one Level-1 predictor and cross-level interaction), values tended to remain below |10%|.
This calls into question how much of a substantive impact such biases would have across common research use cases in psychology, which often emphasize significance testing over precise estimation.
In other words, the fact that complex models may be nominally more biased in their parameter estimation may have little appreciable impact given how these models are used in psychology.
With that said, for certain research implications (e.g., precision modeling), these biases may be enough to substantively affect conclusions.
Serious bias problems (>|10|%) emerged primarily for variance components under certain conditions.
text.formatted: Serious bias problems (>|10|%) emerged primarily for variance components under certain conditions.

text.text: Random intercept variance (τ 00 ) was especially biased when ICC was low (0.1), and all random slope variances (τ 11 , τ²2 , τ 33 ) were highly biased when Level-1 sample sizes were small (n = 5).
Imbalance in Level-1 units increased bias for most parameters, but effects were most pronounced for the variance components.
These patterns suggest that parameter recovery for variance components is more sensitive to sample size structure and ICC than for fixed effects, particularly when estimating multiple random slopes.
Consequently, variance-component estimates under small-sample or imbalanced conditions are unlikely to represent reliable features of the population data-generating process.

This tracks with prior studies (Cools, den Noortgate, & Onghena, 2009; Lee & Hong, 2021), though it is worth noting that those prior investigations emphasize the importance of sample size and ICC over imbalance.
text.formatted: This tracks with prior studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Cools, den Noortgate, & Onghena, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lee & Hong, 2021)</ref>, though it is worth noting that those prior investigations emphasize the importance of sample size and ICC over imbalance.

text.text: Researchers with a strong interest in studying variance components should thus ensure they have large Level-2 sample sizes and avoid extreme case imbalance.

Main-effects analyses of non-coverage revealed that fixed effects were generally well-covered, with only modest increases above the nominal 5% non-coverage rate (typically less than 7-8%) under specific conditions.
Cross-level interactions were more sensitive to variance explained by fixed effects, but visual inspection of non-coverage plots indicated small absolute differences between conditions.
In contrast, variance components showed consistently high non-coverage.
Random slope variances, in particular, exhibited substantial non-coverage inflation under low n, high imbalance, or low ICC.
The Level-1 error variance (σ 2 e ) was most affected by small n, though ICC, N, and imbalance also played significant roles.

This underscores a growing notion in the multilevel modeling literature that increasingly complicated modeling specifications are subject to various considerations that are idiosyncratic to individual models and datasets.
On the flip side, however, these results also underscore the fact that the overall model itself-i.e., every single model component-does not become uniformly worse with increasing complexity.
More broadly, these results converge with and extend a growing body of methodological work on sample-size planning and parameter estimation for multilevel models.
First, these data highlight that Level-2 sample size and extreme case imbalance are the key determinants of variance-component accuracy and CI coverage (Westfall et al., 2014; Murayama et al., 2022).
text.formatted: First, these data highlight that Level-2 sample size and extreme case imbalance are the key determinants of variance-component accuracy and CI coverage <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Westfall et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Murayama et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Second, they emphasize that models with cross-level interactions and multiple random slopes demand a balance of information at both levels to achieve stable estimation (Judd et al., 2017; Mathieu et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Second, they emphasize that models with cross-level interactions and multiple random slopes demand a balance of information at both levels to achieve stable estimation <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Judd et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Mathieu et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, our results highlight that interactions among model specifications, design elements, and population parameters (e.g., ICC) can produce complex, non-linear effects on bias and non-coverage rates (Astivia et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Finally, our results highlight that interactions among model specifications, design elements, and population parameters (e.g., ICC) can produce complex, non-linear effects on bias and non-coverage rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Astivia et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these converging lines of evidence suggest a set of broad motifs, rather than strict guidelines, for future best practices.

First, bias and non-coverage tend to be higher when both the number of Level-2 units and the within-unit sample sizes are small; no single "magic number" (such as N = 50) guarantees stability across modeling contexts.
Second, model complexity increases the inaccuracy of the model estimates, particularly variance components.

Third, while fixed-effect estimates are relatively robust, variance components remain fragile under realistic imbalances, reinforcing the need for replication, sensitivity analyses, and transparent reporting of ICCs and random-effect variances and covariances.
Critically, these motifs concern only the lowest bar of accurate parameter estimation and confidence interval coverage, as they do not directly address statistical power.

The sample sizes needed to reliably recover population parameters are thus a floor, not a ceiling, and researchers should expect that achieving adequate power to detect effects of interest may require considerably larger samples than those needed to ensure estimation accuracy.
The present findings resist simple translation into universal rules of thumb, and we caution against interpreting them as such.

The extension reveals that sample size adequacy is highly context-dependent: the same N and n that yield problematic variance-component coverage under low ICC and high imbalance may perform acceptably when the ICC is large and the design is balanced.

This is particularly relevant for longitudinal and growth-curve applications, which tend to exhibit substantially higher ICCs than those examined in Maas and Hox (2005) and in the extension, contexts in which our results suggest considerably more optimistic performance than a blanket rule would imply.
text.formatted: This is particularly relevant for longitudinal and growth-curve applications, which tend to exhibit substantially higher ICCs than those examined in <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> and in the extension, contexts in which our results suggest considerably more optimistic performance than a blanket rule would imply.

text.text: Rather than prescribing minimum sample sizes, we encourage researchers to use tools like the mlmpower package (Enders et al., 2023) to conduct prospective, model-specific power analyses that incorporate their anticipated ICC, effect sizes expressed as variance explained, and degree of anticipated imbalance.
text.formatted: Rather than prescribing minimum sample sizes, we encourage researchers to use tools like the mlmpower package <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Enders et al., 2023)</ref> to conduct prospective, model-specific power analyses that incorporate their anticipated ICC, effect sizes expressed as variance explained, and degree of anticipated imbalance.

text.text: Balanced designs should be preferred whenever feasible, and researchers with a primary interest in variance components (particularly multiple random slopes) should be especially attentive to both Level-1 and Level-2 sample size.
We also recommend that researchers report their model outputs more thoroughly, specifically following the guidelines specified by McCoach (2019).
text.formatted: We also recommend that researchers report their model outputs more thoroughly, specifically following the guidelines specified by <ref type="bibr">McCoach (2019)</ref>.

text.text: Foremost, this means researchers ought to clearly report their Level-1 and Level-2 sample sizes.

In instances where imbalance exists, they should take care to detail the distribution of Level-1 sample sizes, including the mean, standard deviation, and range of Level-1 sample sizes (and include visualizations if possible).
Researchers should then report the ICC, full variance components and degrees of freedom.

If possible researchers should include an appropriately notated model equation of the model and code snippets in manuscripts or supplements to help ensure that others unambiguously understand how the reported model was specified.
Limitations & Future Directions.
text.formatted: Limitations & Future Directions.

text.text: Two deviations from our preregistered analysis plan merit consideration.

First, identification issues in high-complexity, low n, imbalanced designs required dropping a subset of conditions; this may mean that our results underrepresent the most extreme modeling challenges.

Second, the volume and complexity of interaction effects in the planned logistic regressions proved impractical to interpret meaningfully, leading us to focus on main effects supplemented by cell-level visualizations.
While these changes do not affect the central conclusions, they limit our ability to comment on nuanced interaction patterns among design factors.

Future work could address these limitations by developing more targeted simulations of problematic parameter combinations (e.g., multiple random slopes with high imbalance) and by examining how correlations between random slopes and intercepts influence bias and coverage.

Extending our approach described here would also be helpful, specifically to generalized linear mixed models, multilevel structural equation models, and three-level designs would further align simulation evidence with contemporary applied practice.

In the same vein, we note our use of Wald confidence intervals as a limitation that could be remedied in follow-up studies by leverage other approaches such as resampling methods or profile confidence intervals.
A final consideration worth raising for future simulation researchers concerns the specification of plausible parameter values.

Simulations of multilevel models, whether for substantive use cases or for empirical quantitative research, have historically specified fixed effect coefficients and variance components in isolation, without carefully considering their combined implications.

This matters because often the implied R² values and proportion of variance explained by various model components that follow from a given parameter configuration may be unrealistic relative to what is observed in actual data.
A simulation that specifies individually plausible coefficients can nonetheless imply an overall model that explains an implausibly large proportion of outcome variance.

We therefore encourage future simulators to explicitly derive and report the implied variance-explained quantities associated with their chosen parameter values -as we attempted to do in our extension via the framework of Rights and Sterba (2019) -and to benchmark those values against empirical estimates from the relevant literature.

Doing so would help ensure that simulation conditions reflect the data-generating processes researchers actually encounter in practice, and would strengthen the generalizability of recommendations derived from such work.

Overall, our literature review indicates that many published studies employ models more complex than those evaluated in Maas and Hox (2005) and do so under different conditions (e.g., imbalanced designs, greater ICC values), yet still rely on the original N = 50 guideline.
text.formatted: Overall, our literature review indicates that many published studies employ models more complex than those evaluated in <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Maas and Hox (2005)</ref> and do so under different conditions (e.g., imbalanced designs, greater ICC values), yet still rely on the original N = 50 guideline.

text.text: Our extension suggests that continued reliance on their original recommendations may underestimate the sample sizes needed to ensure accurate variance component estimation and coverage.

Fixed effect parameters for relatively complex models (those involving multiple Level-1 slopes and cross-level interactions) are at risk of modest increases in parameter bias, but in ways that are dependent on modeling application.
We recommend researchers use case-specific tools to better understand the implications of sample size on modeling strategy for their studies.

In our extension, we varied the number of Level-1 predictors and cross-level interactions, manipulated the degree of imbalance in Level-1 sample sizes, simulated across a wider range of ICC values, and generated population parameters based on variance explained.

These design choices were guided by our literature review showing that most contemporary multilevel applications depart substantially from the model used by the original Maas and Hox simulation study (balanced design, one Level-1 and Level-2 predictor each, one cross-level interaction).
